newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. won't push Israel on settlements - analysts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. won't push Israel on settlements - analysts.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may ruffle feathers in Washington by expanding Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza but is unlikely to draw heavy U.S. fire, Israeli analysts said on Thursday.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk assured Netanyahu on Wednesday that the United States had not toughened its long-standing position that settlements pose an "obstacle" to peace, an embassy spokesman said.
They met after U.S. and Israeli spokesmen traded barbs this week over Israel's decision to build 1,200 new homes in Emmanuel settlement in the West Bank, near PLO-ruled Nablus.

"As long as Israel keeps to the policy of allowing natural growth within existing settlements, the Palestinians will protest but the U.S. will not do anything about it," Mark Heller of Tel Aviv's Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies said.
Netanyahu enraged Palestinians when he scrapped a four-year freeze on Jewish settlement construction in occupied Arab lands shortly after his right-wing Likud party came to power in June.
Palestinians view Jewish settlements in territories where they hope to build an independent state as a provocation and vehemently oppose any increase in their numbers.
Some 130,000 Jews have settled amidst more than two million Palestinians since Israel seized the West Bank and Gaza in 1967.
Israel's settlement policies sparked an acrimonious feud with its American ally the last time a Likud government was at the Jewish state's helm in the early 1990s.
But analysts doubt a replay of that spat when U.S. President George Bush rebuffed Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir's request for $10 billion in American loan guarantees.
"In the previous major confrontation between Shamir and Bush, the issue was not expansion of settlements but the creation of new ones," political scientist Eitan Gilboa said.
"The present government is not likely to create new settlements but it is likely to invest more in existing ones," he told Reuters.

Netanyahu has approved the construction of thousands of new homes for Jews in the West Bank since August. But, much to the chagrin of settler groups that helped him come to power, he has not gone ahead with plans for new settlements.
"Netanyahu's pro-settlement rhetoric exceeds what is happening on the ground and that is the source of the clash with the settler right wing," Heller said.
American policy has not changed despite Palestinian hopes for U.S. pressure to nudge a right-wing Israel along the peace path set out by Israel's previous left-centre administration.
"Ambassador Indyk told Israel yesterday the policy has not changed. We have the same formulation as during the previous Labour government," U.S. embassy spokesman Richard Scorza said.
"We have never found the settlements helpful in peace negotiations and we find that they present an obstacle to carrying out the search for a solution," Scorza told Reuters.

Under a 1993 Israel-PLO peace deal, the fate of Jewish settlements will be determined in talks on a final peace accord to be completed by 1999, along with other thorny issues such as borders between Israel and a future Palestinian entity.

"There seems to be some kind of vague, tacit understanding of the principle that the largest settlements will be attached to Israel under a final peace with the Palestinians," Heller said, describing a possible deal the PLO says it will oppose.
He said he saw few reasons for the United States to alter its policy.
"The policy has been consistent enough to have some credibility but ambiguous enough to accept developments that aren't excessively disruptive," said Heller.
